pr_title: homed: flush fscrypt key on lock/deactivate
pr_body:
The fscrypt key is added to the user keyring, and needs to be flushed out too.

Fixes https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/33138























<!-- devel-freezer = {"comment-id":"2146445388","freezing-tag":"v256-rc3"} -->
pr_comments:
> [!NOTE]
> We had successfully released a new major release. We are no longer in a development freeze phase.
> We will try our best to get back to your PR as soon as possible. Thank you for your patience.

I am not sure i grok why this is even necessary. i.e. the per-user keyring should go away automatically when the kernel does not see any process owned by the keyring owner's key anymore.

hence, how come the keyring remains pinned for the original poster?
I don't think we need to hurry this into v256. This isn't really a regression.

> I am not sure i grok why this is even necessary. i.e. the per-user keyring should go away automatically when the kernel does not see any process owned by the keyring owner's key anymore.
> 
> hence, how come the keyring remains pinned for the original poster?

I don't know - but it's easily reproducible, it is there with the home deactivated and the user logged out

> I don't think we need to hurry this into v256. This isn't really a regression.

It isn't, however one of the key selling point of homed is to drop private key material from memory when the user is logged out, so I thought it would be good to fix anyway since it's not too difficult. It's also self-contained to homed+fscrypt and all done in a forked process, so should be as safe as it could be.

> I don't know - but it's easily reproducible, it is there with the home deactivated and the user logged out

well, what i am saying is that there probably is something else wrong here, if the the thing doesn#t get cleaned up automatically by the kernel

So I am pretty sure there's some other bug lurking somewhere if the kernel doesn't clean this up automatically, but it might be ok to clean-up a user's keyring explicitly if we assume the user is fully logged out.

But I am pretty sure this should be dumbed down, and not be placed in homed, but logind, i.e. in user_finalize() at the same place where we call clean_ipc_by_uid().

This should really delete *all* keys of the user, i.e. fire a "clear" operation (KEYCTL_CLEAR).

> So I am pretty sure there's some other bug lurking somewhere if the kernel doesn't clean this up automatically, but it might be ok to clean-up a user's keyring explicitly if we assume the user is fully logged out.
> 
> But I am pretty sure this should be dumbed down, and not be placed in homed, but logind, i.e. in user_finalize() at the same place where we call clean_ipc_by_uid().
> 
> This should really delete _all_ keys of the user, i.e. fire a "clear" operation (KEYCTL_CLEAR).

Doing this in logind doesn't help with `homectl activate` -> `homectl deactivate` though, no? This specific issue is about the combination of homed+fscrypt, and it's homed that puts this key in the keyring, so it seems right to me that it's homed that removes it once it is not needed, just like it removes the other stuff from the keyrings. If issues with other things handled by logind show up then we can handle it there and then, but I think this fix should be targeted to this specific bug.
This looks better, but the (automatic, I assume) formatting is still rather ugly.

> This looks better, but the (automatic, I assume) formatting is still rather ugly.

Updated - but the issue is that this changes depending on who's reviewing. Some want multiple parameters per line starting on the same line, some want one parameter per line starting on the next line. We should really just get clang-formatter going and enforce it via CI and let that be the end of it...

I think you're looking at this from the wrong angle. Code is something that is read much more than it is written. Thus, self-consistent, legible, clean code is worth a bit of extra formatting effort. Clang-format and other tools can be a useful tool, especially for beginners and a new codebase, but are not powerful enough for us.

FWIW, people tried to build a clang format specification before, and it always fell short.

Exactly - the problem is that "self-consistent, legible, clean" are in the eye of the beholder, so depending on who happens to review a PR, requirements change, which is not great. If it's enforced by a tool, then you cannot argue against the tool (well you can try, but the tool will just look at you with a funny face)

That'd mean having ugly formatting. If people want to use clang format or some other helper, that's fine. It's up to them, as long as they fix the most egregious shortcomings. But making this enforced is a completely different thing.  That'd force people who want and can do better to commit badly formatted code.

issue_context.title: fscrypt key appears to still be active after logout
issue_context.body:
### systemd version the issue has been seen with

256~rc3-6

### Used distribution

debian unstable

### Linux kernel version used

6.8.11-amd64

### CPU architectures issue was seen on

x86_64

### Component

systemd-homed

### Expected behaviour you didn't see

following up from #32596, i'm experimenting with fscrypt-backed home directories created and maintained by `systemd-homed`.

It looks to me like the fscrypt key is not being correctly dropped.

according to `keyrings(7)`, `/proc/keys` is supposed to report different information depending on the permissions of the thread accessing it.

I don't really understand how to parse this file, but i tried to access it as user `moogly`, uid 60240.  I think i've run into some other bug with `sudo` here, because:

Enable fscrypt if needed and create a user:

```
# tune2fs -O encrypt /dev/device
# homectl create --storage=fscrypt moogly
```

```
0 root@unstable-amd64:~# sudo -u moogly -- id -u
[sudo] password for %p: 
60240
0 root@unstable-amd64:~# 
```

i just hit enter -- did not enter the password for `moogly` -- at the strange-looking prompt.

Anyway, to avoid any risk that `sudo` might try to tickle the PAM or NSS stacks, which in turn might tickle `systemd` and do something related to the fscrypt homedir, i figured i'd look at `/proc/keys` using `chpst` from [runit](https://smarden.org/runit/), version 2.1.2-59.  My understanding is that `chpst` is bare-bones.

Using that, it appears that `moogly`'s `fscrypt` key is still present after logout ☹.

### Unexpected behaviour you saw

As in #32596, ⛳ prefixes a one-line comment about the state of the system.

```
⛳ fresh boot
0 root@unstable-amd64:~# chpst -u :60240:60240 cat /proc/keys
00686174 I--Q---     4 perm 1f3f0000     0 65534 keyring   _uid.0: empty
2fc4b570 I--Q---     9 perm 3f030000     0     0 keyring   _ses: 1
⛳ moogly logs in
0 root@unstable-amd64:~# chpst -u :60240:60240 cat /proc/keys
00686174 I--Q---     4 perm 1f3f0000     0 65534 keyring   _uid.0: empty
1da94d1f I--Q---     1 perm 3d010000 60240 60240 logon     fscrypt:54c5eb495739a0b6: 72
25815ea1 I--Q---     4 perm 1f3f0000 60240 65534 keyring   _uid.60240: 1
2664d714 I--Q---     1 perm 1f3f0000 60240 65534 keyring   _uid_ses.60240: 1
2fc4b570 I--Q---     9 perm 3f030000     0     0 keyring   _ses: 1
31d695c6 I--Q---     5 perm 3f030000 60240 60240 keyring   _ses: 1
34548126 I--Q---     4 perm 3f030000 60240 60240 keyring   _ses: 1
⛳ moogly does "cat test.txt"
0 root@unstable-amd64:~# chpst -u :60240:60240 cat /proc/keys
00686174 I--Q---     4 perm 1f3f0000     0 65534 keyring   _uid.0: empty
1da94d1f I--Q---     1 perm 3d010000 60240 60240 logon     fscrypt:54c5eb495739a0b6: 72
25815ea1 I--Q---     4 perm 1f3f0000 60240 65534 keyring   _uid.60240: 1
2664d714 I--Q---     1 perm 1f3f0000 60240 65534 keyring   _uid_ses.60240: 1
2fc4b570 I--Q---     9 perm 3f030000     0     0 keyring   _ses: 1
31d695c6 I--Q---     5 perm 3f030000 60240 60240 keyring   _ses: 1
34548126 I--Q---     4 perm 3f030000 60240 60240 keyring   _ses: 1
⛳ moogly logs out, wait 5 seconds
0 root@unstable-amd64:~# chpst -u :60240:60240 cat /proc/keys
00686174 I--Q---     4 perm 1f3f0000     0 65534 keyring   _uid.0: empty
1da94d1f I--Q---     1 perm 3d010000 60240 60240 logon     fscrypt:54c5eb495739a0b6: 72
25815ea1 I--Q---     3 perm 1f3f0000 60240 65534 keyring   _uid.60240: 1
2664d714 I--Q---     1 perm 1f3f0000 60240 65534 keyring   _uid_ses.60240: 1
2fc4b570 I--Q---     9 perm 3f030000     0     0 keyring   _ses: 1
31d695c6 I--Q---     5 perm 3f030000 60240 60240 keyring   _ses: 1
⛳ wait another 10 minutes
0 root@unstable-amd64:~# chpst -u :60240:60240 cat /proc/keys
00686174 I--Q---     4 perm 1f3f0000     0 65534 keyring   _uid.0: empty
1da94d1f I--Q---     1 perm 3d010000 60240 60240 logon     fscrypt:54c5eb495739a0b6: 72
25815ea1 I--Q---     2 perm 1f3f0000 60240 65534 keyring   _uid.60240: 1
2664d714 I--Q---     1 perm 1f3f0000 60240 65534 keyring   _uid_ses.60240: 1
2fc4b570 I--Q---     9 perm 3f030000     0     0 keyring   _ses: 1
0 root@unstable-amd64:~# 
```

So yes, it appears that some keys are still held by user `60240`, including one with an `fscrypt:` prefix.

If you need me to debug further, please suggest what i should do.

### Steps to reproduce the problem

- following the same steps as #32596 to set up the system.
- `apt install --no-install-recommends runit`
- as `root`, examine the state of `/proc/keys` while `moogly` logs in and logs out.

### Additional program output to the terminal or log subsystem illustrating the issue

_No response_
comments:
```
Jun 04 00:09:35 localhost systemd-homework[943]: Syncing completed.
Jun 04 00:09:35 localhost systemd-homework[943]: Umounting /run/systemd/user-home-mount...
Jun 04 00:09:35 localhost systemd-homework[943]: Unmounting completed.
Jun 04 00:09:35 localhost systemd-homework[943]: Failed to find kernel keyring entry for user, ignoring: Required key not available
Jun 04 00:09:35 localhost systemd-homework[943]: Dropped caches.
Jun 04 00:09:36 localhost kernel: systemd-homewor (943): drop_caches: 3
Jun 04 00:09:35 localhost systemd-homework[943]: Everything completed.
```

Looks like flushing the keyring fails as the key can't be found, for some reason

Actually flushing the fscrypt key is not implemented at all, so this is not really a regression. It's a 'logon' keyring, which according to the kernel doc makes it unreadable from userspace so it's probably not too bad.

So, my understanding is that the per-user keyring goes away anyway if the last process of the owning user goes away. Hence how come this is not cleaned up automatically for you?

do you have a process hidden somewhere that is owned by the user in question?

> So, my understanding is that the per-user keyring goes away anyway if the last process of the owning user goes away. Hence how come this is not cleaned up automatically for you?
> 
> do you have a process hidden somewhere that is owned by the user in question?

No processes or sessions left. This is trivially reproducible with a mkosi mage built on latest main btw, just build it, add a user with `homectl create --storage=fscrypt test`, and then activate it with homectl, and deactivate it again - no need to even login. The fscrypt key will be in the user keyring.

As per man page user-keyring(7):

> The user keyring is associated with the record that the kernel maintains for the UID.  It comes into existence upon the first attempt to access either the user keyring, the user-session-keyring(7), or the  session-keyring(7). The  keyring  remains  pinned  in  existence  so  long as there are processes running with that real UID or files opened by those processes remain open.  (The keyring can also be pinned indefinitely by linking it into another keyring.)

So, it relaly should be cleaned up automatically.

> (The keyring can also be pinned indefinitely by linking it into another keyring.)

Are we linking it somewhere else maybe?

Thanks for fixing this!  The `fscrypt` key is now purged, but something else is still holding a couple keys for the user even 10 minutes after they log out.  I've opened #33308 to track that remaining concern.

review_comments: It'd be nicer to move the implementation of child into a separate function that does a normal negative return. All those `_exit(EXIT_FAILURE)` calls are overly verbose and error-prone.

this one is ok to stay at debug level
we have this same loop twice now, can we please get a helper call for this, i.e. add a helper to src/shared/keyring-util.c called keyring_describe() or so, that does this describe loop.
